title: Detection of Threat Intel Vendors
summary: This detection strategy covers the search for threat intelligence vendors, the technique where an adversary identifies which commercial intelligence, brand monitoring or incident response providers the target uses, so they can avoid detection or pick a victim who is poorly monitored. It matters because the collection is mostly off network: it shows up as unusual reads of the organisation's own public security pages, supplier lists and job adverts that mention a product, plus requests to security vendor comparison sites and reseller portals from corporate addresses. The telemetry that makes it possible is web proxy and content delivery logs with the requested path and user agent, domain name system query logs for vendor and comparison domains, marketing site analytics with referrer and address data, and open source monitoring of brand mentions. Detection fails because security teams legitimately research vendors all day, and because much of this reconnaissance happens through third party sites the defender does not control.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for someone working out which security companies protect your business. Attackers want to know what monitoring you use. The rule watches for unusual visits to vendor pages, reseller sites and comparison websites. It can also watch public mentions of your tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker knows your security products, they can choose methods those products miss. Public pages, job adverts and conference talks often name those products. This is quiet research, not an intrusion. Noticing it early tells you that someone is studying your defences.
howItWorks: Web requests from company devices are logged. The log holds the site, the page path, the user agent and the user.
Requests are grouped by the domain category, so known security vendor and comparison sites are easy to select.
The rule counts how many different vendor or reseller pages one user visits in a window.
It compares the count with the normal pattern for that user and for the security team.
Marketing site analytics show when one external address reads many of your product and supplier pages.
Alerts join the two views, so an internal reader and an external scraper can be seen as one campaign.
beginner.example: Think of a shoplifter who first reads the shop sign to learn which security firm watches the cameras. Knowing the firm tells the thief which blind spots to expect. Reading the sign is not a crime, yet it changes what happens next. This detection watches who keeps reading the sign.
takeaways: Security vendor research is quiet and often done through public pages.
Job adverts and conference talks leak your tooling, so review them as part of exposure.
A short burst of vendor page reads by one account is worth a look, not an incident.

objectives: Explain why knowing the defender's tooling helps an adversary avoid detection.
Identify the proxy, analytics and resolver fields that show vendor research.
Write a rule that counts distinct vendor and comparison domains per user in a window.
Describe how to review public material that names your security suppliers.
Explain how this collection supports later defence evasion choices.
dataSources: Secure web gateway logs with requested host, uniform resource locator path, user agent and authenticated user
Web server and content delivery logs for the corporate public site showing referrer, address and requested pages
Domain name system resolver logs for security vendor, reseller and product comparison domains
Marketing automation and site analytics records listing which external addresses read product and supplier pages
Open source brand monitoring feeds that report new public mentions of the organisation and its tools
logic: The pattern is one internal identity or one external address reading many pages that describe security products, resellers, comparison reviews and supplier lists inside a short window, especially when the requested paths go deeper than the landing page and the same address or account also reads job adverts that name tooling. The fields that must be correlated are the authenticated user or external address, the distinct vendor and comparison domains or paths requested, the user agent and client, the referrer chain, and the identity's normal browsing profile. The benign case is a security engineer evaluating products, which is sustained over days and matched by downloads of datasheets; the malicious case is a tight burst of vendor and comparison page reads by an account that never visits these sites, often from a hosting address or through a proxy, combined with reads of your public security pages.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Security Vendor and Comparison Site Research Burst
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: web_proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'security-vendor-directory'
#       - 'siem-comparison'
#       - 'endpoint-protection-review'
#   filter_security_team:
#     user|endswith: 'security'
#   condition: selection and not filter_security_team | count(distinct url) by user > 25 within 2h
# level: low
falsePositives: Security engineers evaluating replacement products during a planned procurement review
Analysts reading industry comparison articles while preparing an internal briefing
Marketing staff monitoring how competitors and partners present the company on review sites
A recruiter checking whether candidates have experience with specific security products
tuningNotes: Scope the alert to accounts outside the security, information technology and procurement teams, and require a mix of vendor, reseller and review domains rather than one repeated site so a single long article does not trigger it. Baseline the domain categories each team visits for thirty days and alert on new categories rather than raw counts. Add the public site analytics side as a separate low severity rule keyed on one external address reading many supplier pages. Because the filter excludes the security team, you lose visibility of a compromised security account doing the same research, so keep a monthly report of vendor page reads for those accounts and review it manually.
